claim: Socially-conveyed rules and instructions strongly shape expectations and emotions.
source: Socially-conveyed rules and instructions strongly shape expectations and emotions.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that sets up the research context.

claim: Most neuroscientific studies of learning consider reinforcement history alone, irrespective of knowledge acquired through other means.
source: Yet most neuroscientific studies of learning consider reinforcement history alone, irrespective of knowledge acquired through other means.
evidence: This is a characterization of the existing literature that motivates the study.

claim: Instructions induced dissociations in the neural systems of aversive learning.
source: We combined quantitative models with functional magnetic resonance imaging and found that instructions induced dissociations in the neural systems of aversive learning.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on fMRI and modeling data.

claim: Responses in striatum and orbitofrontal cortex updated with instructions and correlated with prefrontal responses to instructions.
source: Responses in striatum and orbitofrontal cortex updated with instructions and correlated with prefrontal responses to instructions.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on fMRI data.

claim: Amygdala responses were influenced by reinforcement similarly in both groups and did not update with instructions.
source: Amygdala responses were influenced by reinforcement similarly in both groups and did not update with instructions.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study based on fMRI data comparing groups.

claim: Results extend work on instructed reward learning.
source: Results extend work on instructed reward learning and reveal novel dissociations that have not been observed with punishments or rewards.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in relation to prior literature.

claim: Findings reveal novel dissociations that have not been observed with punishments or rewards.
source: Results extend work on instructed reward learning and reveal novel dissociations that have not been observed with punishments or rewards.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings relative to prior work.

claim: Findings support theories of specialized threat-detection.
source: Findings support theories of specialized threat-detection and may have implications for fear maintenance in anxiety.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in relation to theoretical frameworks.

claim: Findings may have implications for fear maintenance in anxiety.
source: Findings support theories of specialized threat-detection and may have implications for fear maintenance in anxiety.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential clinical implications.

claim: Brain systems that govern learning from punishments and rewards seem to be largely conserved across species.
source: Neuroscientists have built a rich understanding of the brain systems that govern learning from punishments and rewards, which seem to be largely conserved across species (Balleine and O'Doherty, 2010; Haber and Knutson, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Humans possess a distinctive capacity to learn from socially-conveyed rules and instructions.
source: Yet humans possess a distinctive capacity to learn from socially-conveyed rules and instructions, which is an important example of a broader capacity, shared by many species, of learning from events other than simple reinforcers (Tolman, 1949).
evidence: This is supported by citation and general knowledge about human cognition.

claim: The capacity to learn from socially-conveyed rules is an example of a broader capacity, shared by many species, of learning from events other than simple reinforcers.
source: Yet humans possess a distinctive capacity to learn from socially-conveyed rules and instructions, which is an important example of a broader capacity, shared by many species, of learning from events other than simple reinforcers (Tolman, 1949).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tolman (1949).

claim: Most reinforcement learning models fail to account for the potential influence of explicit information.
source: It is unknown whether instructions integrate with the systems that support error-driven learning, as most reinforcement learning models fail to account for the potential influence of explicit information, despite the fact that verbal information shapes responses across nearly all domains, including aversive learning (Wilson, 1968; Phelps et al., 2001; Costa et al., 2015; Mertens and De Houwer, 2016).
evidence: This is a characterization of the modeling literature.

claim: Verbal information shapes responses across nearly all domains, including aversive learning.
source: It is unknown whether instructions integrate with the systems that support error-driven learning, as most reinforcement learning models fail to account for the potential influence of explicit information, despite the fact that verbal information shapes responses across nearly all domains, including aversive learning (Wilson, 1968; Phelps et al., 2001; Costa et al., 2015; Mertens and De Houwer, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Instructions about rewarding outcomes modulate learning-related responses in the striatum.
source: Recent studies in the appetitive domain suggest that instructions about rewarding outcomes modulate learning-related responses in the striatum (Doll et al., 2009; 2011; Li et al., 2011a) and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (Li et al., 2011a) and that this modulation might depend on the prefrontal cortex (Doll et al., 2009; 2011; Li et al., 2011a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Instructions about rewarding outcomes modulate learning-related responses in the ventromedial prefrontal cortex.
source: Recent studies in the appetitive domain suggest that instructions about rewarding outcomes modulate learning-related responses in the striatum (Doll et al., 2009; 2011; Li et al., 2011a) and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (Li et al., 2011a) and that this modulation might depend on the prefrontal cortex (Doll et al., 2009; 2011; Li et al., 2011a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2011a.

claim: Modulation of learning-related responses by instructions might depend on the prefrontal cortex.
source: Recent studies in the appetitive domain suggest that instructions about rewarding outcomes modulate learning-related responses in the striatum (Doll et al., 2009; 2011; Li et al., 2011a) and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (Li et al., 2011a) and that this modulation might depend on the prefrontal cortex (Doll et al., 2009; 2011; Li et al., 2011a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Dynamic aversive learning is known to depend on the amygdala.
source: However, no studies have tested whether instructions have the same effects on dynamic aversive learning, which is known to depend on the amygdala (Maren, 2001) but also involves the striatum (Seymour et al., 2004; 2005; Delgado et al., 2008b) and ventromedial/orbitofrontal cortex (VMPFC/OFC) (Phelps et al., 2004; Kalisch et al., 2006; Schiller et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Maren, 2001.

claim: Dynamic aversive learning involves the striatum.
source: However, no studies have tested whether instructions have the same effects on dynamic aversive learning, which is known to depend on the amygdala (Maren, 2001) but also involves the striatum (Seymour et al., 2004; 2005; Delgado et al., 2008b) and ventromedial/orbitofrontal cortex (VMPFC/OFC) (Phelps et al., 2004; Kalisch et al., 2006; Schiller et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Dynamic aversive learning involves the ventromedial/orbitofrontal cortex.
source: However, no studies have tested whether instructions have the same effects on dynamic aversive learning, which is known to depend on the amygdala (Maren, 2001) but also involves the striatum (Seymour et al., 2004; 2005; Delgado et al., 2008b) and ventromedial/orbitofrontal cortex (VMPFC/OFC) (Phelps et al., 2004; Kalisch et al., 2006; Schiller et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Amygdala responses might be insensitive to cognitive instruction, as suggested by theories of automatic threat detection in the amygdala.
source: Instructions might modulate learning in the amygdala as well as the striatum and VMPFC/OFC, or amygdala responses might be insensitive to cognitive instruction (Ohman and Mineka, 2001), as suggested by theories of automatic threat detection in the amygdala (Ohman, 2005).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to theoretical work.

claim: One image (the Original CS+) was paired with mild electric shock on 30% of trials.
source: All participants performed a Pavlovian aversive learning task in which one image, the Original conditioned stimulus (CS+), was paired with mild electric shock (the unconditioned stimulus [US]) on 30% of trials, and a second image, the Original CS-, was not paired with shock.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: A second image (the Original CS-) was not paired with shock.
source: All participants performed a Pavlovian aversive learning task in which one image, the Original conditioned stimulus (CS+), was paired with mild electric shock (the unconditioned stimulus [US]) on 30% of trials, and a second image, the Original CS-, was not paired with shock.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Contingencies reversed three times during the task.
source: Contingencies reversed three times.
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Participants assigned to an Instructed Group were informed about initial contingencies and instructed upon reversal.
source: Participants assigned to an Instructed Group were informed about initial contingencies and instructed upon reversal (Figure 1), whereas participants in an Uninstructed Group learned through reinforcement alone.
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation.

claim: Participants in an Uninstructed Group learned through reinforcement alone.
source: Participants assigned to an Instructed Group were informed about initial contingencies and instructed upon reversal (Figure 1), whereas participants in an Uninstructed Group learned through reinforcement alone.
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation.

claim: SCRs updated immediately with instructions.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Wilson, 1968; Grings et al., 1973), SCRs updated immediately with instructions.
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data and consistent with prior literature.

claim: Both groups showed differential responses that reversed in response to contingency changes throughout the task (CS+ > CS-).
source: As reported in Table 1, both groups showed differential responses that reversed in response to contingency changes throughout the task (CS+ > CS-; ß = 0.04, t = 5.82, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on SCR data.

claim: Differential responses were larger in the Instructed Group than the Uninstructed Group.
source: Differential responses were larger in the Instructed Group than the Uninstructed Group (ß = 0.03, t = 3.98, p=0.0002), and SCRs habituated over time (ß = -0.07, t = 10.59, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on SCR data.

claim: SCRs habituated over time.
source: Differential responses were larger in the Instructed Group than the Uninstructed Group (ß = 0.03, t = 3.98, p=0.0002), and SCRs habituated over time (ß = -0.07, t = 10.59, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on SCR data.

claim: Participants recognized that three reversals had occurred (M = 3.22, SD = 0.79).
source: Participants recognized that three reversals had occurred (M = 3.22, SD = 0.79), and there was no group difference in the estimated number of reversals (p>0.1).
evidence: This is a finding from subjective ratings.

claim: There was no group difference in the estimated number of reversals.
source: Participants recognized that three reversals had occurred (M = 3.22, SD = 0.79), and there was no group difference in the estimated number of reversals (p>0.1).
evidence: This is a finding from subjective ratings.

claim: The Uninstructed Group reported less positive affect for both stimuli.
source: Two-way ANOVAs revealed a main effect of Group on reported affect (F(1,68) = 8.57, p<0.01), such that the Uninstructed Group reported less positive affect for both stimuli.
evidence: This is a finding from subjective ratings.

claim: There were no Group differences in shock expectancy ratings.
source: There were no Group differences in shock expectancy ratings, nor were there any main effects of Stimulus (Original CS+ vs Original CS-) or Group x Stimulus interactions on either outcome measure.
evidence: This is a finding from subjective ratings.

claim: The best-fitting parameters when fit across Instructed Group subjects revealed that EV reversed almost completely at the time of instructions in the Instructed Group (ρ = 0.943).
source: The best-fitting parameters when fit across Instructed Group subjects revealed that EV reversed almost completely at the time of instructions in the Instructed Group (ρ = 0.943; Table 2), suggesting that instructions immediately influence EV/SCR, as illustrated in Figure 2B.
evidence: This is a finding from quantitative modeling of SCR data.

claim: When the model was fit to SCRs from the Uninstructed Group, estimates were consistent with associations not reversing at the time when the instructions would have been delivered (ρ = 0.0).
source: When we fit the same model to SCRs from the Uninstructed Group (for whom the additional effect should not be observed since no instructions were given) estimates were indeed consistent with associations not reversing at the time when the instructions would have been delivered (ρ = 0.0; Table 2).
evidence: This is a finding from quantitative modeling of SCR data.

claim: Instructed reversal parameters (ρ) differed significantly as a function of Group (Instructed Group > Uninstructed Group).
source: We also fit the model to individual participants in both groups (see Materials and methods) and found that instructed reversal parameters (i.e. ρ) differed significantly as a function of Group (Instructed Group > Uninstructed Group, t(38) = 6.53, p<0.0001; Table 2).
evidence: This is a finding from quantitative modeling of individual participant data.

claim: ROI-based analyses within the Uninstructed Group revealed positive correlations between feedback-driven EV and responses in the amygdala.
source: ROI-based analyses within the Uninstructed Group revealed a main effect of Region (F(2,40) = 5.13, p=0.011). Post-hoc t-tests revealed that this was driven by positive correlations between feedback-driven EV and responses in the amygdala (bilateral: t(1,19) = 4.21, p=0.0005; Left: t(1, 19) = 3.94, p=0.001; Right: t(1,19): = 3.72, p=0.001) and striatum (bilateral: t(1,19) = 2.31, p=0.0017; left: t(1, 19) = 2.58, p=p =0.018; right: p=p =0.063).
evidence: This is a finding from fMRI ROI analyses.

claim: ROI-based analyses within the Uninstructed Group revealed positive correlations between feedback-driven EV and responses in the striatum.
source: ROI-based analyses within the Uninstructed Group revealed a main effect of Region (F(2,40) = 5.13, p=0.011). Post-hoc t-tests revealed that this was driven by positive correlations between feedback-driven EV and responses in the amygdala (bilateral: t(1,19) = 4.21, p=0.0005; Left: t(1, 19) = 3.94, p=0.001; Right: t(1,19): = 3.72, p=0.001) and striatum (bilateral: t(1,19) = 2.31, p=0.0017; left: t(1, 19) = 2.58, p=p =0.018; right: p=p =0.063).
evidence: This is a finding from fMRI ROI analyses.

claim: Voxel-wise FDR-corrected results confirmed ROI-based findings and isolated additional correlations in the VMPFC/mOFC.
source: Voxel-wise FDR-corrected results confirmed ROI-based findings, and isolated additional correlations in the VMPFC/mOFC (see Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1—source data 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a finding from fMRI voxel-wise analyses.

claim: The VMPFC/mOFC showed negative correlations with EV, consistent with prior work showing increased VMPFC/OFC responses to conditioned stimuli predicting safe, relative to aversive, outcomes.
source: The VMPFC/mOFC showed negative correlations with EV, consistent with prior work showing increased VMPFC/OFC responses to conditioned stimuli predicting safe, relative to aversive, outcomes (Schiller et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a finding from fMRI data that is consistent with prior literature.

claim: ROI-based analyses in the Instructed Group revealed significant negative correlations with instruction-based EV in the VMPFC/OFC ROI.
source: ROI-based ANOVAs revealed a significant effect of Region (F(2,40) = 6.49, p=0.0038), driven by significant negative correlations with EV in the VMPFC/OFC ROI (t(1,19) = -2.61, p=0.0173; see Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from fMRI ROI analyses.

claim: Voxelwise FDR-corrected results revealed robust activation in the bilateral caudate, which showed positive correlations with instructed EV.
source: Voxelwise FDR-corrected results also revealed robust activation in the bilateral caudate, which showed positive correlations with instructed EV (see Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 2—source data 1, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2—source data 2).
evidence: This is a finding from fMRI voxel-wise analyses.

claim: Voxelwise FDR-corrected analyses revealed that the bilateral amygdala was preferentially correlated with feedback-driven EV.
source: Voxelwise FDR-corrected analyses revealed that the bilateral amygdala was preferentially correlated with feedback-driven EV, while the right caudate and left putamen showed preferential correlations with instruction-based EV (see Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding from fMRI voxel-wise analyses comparing models within the Instructed Group.

claim: The right caudate and left putamen showed preferential correlations with instruction-based EV.
source: Voxelwise FDR-corrected analyses revealed that the bilateral amygdala was preferentially correlated with feedback-driven EV, while the right caudate and left putamen showed preferential correlations with instruction-based EV (see Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, and Figure 4—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding from fMRI voxel-wise analyses comparing models within the Instructed Group.

claim: ROI-based analyses confirmed voxelwise results, with amygdala correlations with feedback-driven EV but not instructed EV.
source: ROI-based analyses confirmed voxelwise results, with a main effect of Region (F(2,40) = 3.76, p=0.0324; Figure 4A), driven by amygdala correlations with feedback-driven EV but not instructed EV (t(1,19) = 2.57, p=0.0189), although striatal differences between models were not significant when averaged across the entire ROI.
evidence: This is a finding from fMRI ROI analyses comparing models within the Instructed Group.

claim: A number of regions showed differential responses that reversed upon instruction, including the right VS and VMPFC/OFC.
source: We observed immediate instructed reversal effects in the ventral striatum and VMPFC/OFC. The VMPFC/OFC was identified in both ROI-based and voxel-wise analyses, while the striatal activation was evident in voxel-wise analyses (see Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding from task-based fMRI analyses of instructed reversals.

claim: The VS showed greater activation to the current CS+, relative to the corresponding CS-.
source: Post-hoc analyses revealed that the VS showed greater activation to the current CS+, relative to the corresponding CS-, while VMPFC/OFC showed greater deactivation to the current CS+ (t(1,19) = -4.82, p=p =0.0001).
evidence: This is a finding from task-based fMRI analyses of instructed reversals.

claim: VMPFC/OFC showed greater deactivation to the current CS+.
source: Post-hoc analyses revealed that the VS showed greater activation to the current CS+, relative to the corresponding CS-, while VMPFC/OFC showed greater deactivation to the current CS+ (t(1,19) = -4.82, p=p =0.0001).
evidence: This is a finding from task-based fMRI analyses of instructed reversals.

claim: The right amygdala showed differential responses that did not reverse upon instruction.
source: Voxel-wise analyses revealed that the right amygdala showed differential responses that did not reverse upon instruction (Figure 5B), although effects were not significant when averaged across the entire ROI.
evidence: This is a finding from task-based fMRI analyses of instructed reversals.

claim: The magnitude of the behavioral reversal effect was positively correlated with instructed reversal effects in bilateral dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), bilateral caudate tail and thalamus, dACC, and right anterior insula.
source: We found that the magnitude of the behavioral reversal effect was positively correlated with instructed reversal effects in bilateral dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), bilateral caudate tail and thalamus, dACC, and right anterior insula (see Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 3, and Figure 5—figure supplement 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is a finding from brain-behavior correlation analyses.

claim: Differential responses in the amygdala (which did not reverse with instructions) were strongest in those individuals whose behavior showed the weakest influence of instructions.
source: Conversely, differential responses in the amygdala (which did not reverse with instructions) were strongest in those individuals whose behavior showed the weakest influence of instructions (see Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 3, and Figure 5—figure supplement 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is a finding from brain-behavior correlation analyses.

claim: The left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) showed greater activation across all trials in the Instructed Group at an uncorrected threshold of p<0.001.
source: Although no regions survived FDR-correction, the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC; middle frontal gyrus, peak voxel xyz = [-43 43 21]) showed greater activation across all trials in the Instructed Group at an uncorrected threshold of p<0.001 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is a finding from between-groups fMRI analyses.

claim: Individuals who showed greater DLPFC activation during instruction showed stronger reversals in the right putamen and VMPFC/mOFC.
source: We observed significant positive correlations in the right putamen (peak voxel xyz = [24 8 11]) and negative correlations in the VMPFC/mOFC (peak voxel xyz = [-5 40 -17]; see Figure 6C), although the VMPFC/mOFC cluster was slightly smaller than our cluster threshold (9 voxels rather than 10). In both cases, individuals who showed greater DLPFC activation during instruction showed stronger reversals, with greater activation to the current CS+ than CS- in the putamen, and greater deactivation to the current CS+ in the VMPFC/mOFC.
evidence: This is a finding from brain-behavior correlation analyses linking DLPFC responses to instructed reversals.

claim: Instructions influence reward learning.
source: Recent studies indicate that instructions influence reward learning (Doll et al., 2009; 2011; Li et al., 2011a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: When individuals are instructed about contingencies, the prefrontal cortex influences responses in the striatum.
source: When individuals are instructed about contingencies, the prefrontal cortex influences responses in the striatum (Doll et al., 2009; 2011; Li et al., 2011a), and VMPFC/OFC (Li et al., 2011a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: When individuals are instructed about contingencies, the prefrontal cortex influences responses in the VMPFC/OFC.
source: When individuals are instructed about contingencies, the prefrontal cortex influences responses in the striatum (Doll et al., 2009; 2011; Li et al., 2011a), and VMPFC/OFC (Li et al., 2011a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2011a.

claim: The striatum and VMPFC/OFC make up a well-characterized network that supports error-based learning across both appetitive and aversive domains.
source: The striatum and VMPFC/OFC make up a well-characterized network that supports error-based learning across both appetitive and aversive domains (Balleine and O'Doherty, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Balleine and O'Doherty, 2010.

claim: The VMPFC/OFC has been linked with expected value and reversal learning.
source: The VMPFC/OFC has been linked with expected value and reversal learning (Murray et al., 2007; Schiller et al., 2008; Rudebeck et al., 2013), and the striatum is known to play a critical role in error-based learning (Delgado et al., 2008b; Haber and Knutson, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The striatum is known to play a critical role in error-based learning.
source: The VMPFC/OFC has been linked with expected value and reversal learning (Murray et al., 2007; Schiller et al., 2008; Rudebeck et al., 2013), and the striatum is known to play a critical role in error-based learning (Delgado et al., 2008b; Haber and Knutson, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Striatal activation increased in anticipation of aversive outcomes, whereas the VMPFC/OFC deactivated.
source: While the striatum and VMPFC/OFC both updated with instructions, the valence of responses diverged: Striatal activation increased in anticipation of aversive outcomes, whereas the VMPFC/OFC deactivated.
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on fMRI data.

claim: The VMPFC/OFC represents a valenced outcome expectancy signal, which correlates positively with reward magnitude or the strength of appetitive outcomes.
source: This is consistent with a large number of studies suggesting that the VMPFC/OFC represents a valenced outcome expectancy signal, which correlates positively with reward magnitude or the strength of appetitive outcomes (Montague and Berns, 2002; Rangel and Hare, 2010; Grabenhorst and Rolls, 2011; Clithero and Rangel, 2013), and correlates negatively with the magnitude of aversive outcomes (Schiller et al., 2008; Plassmann et al., 2010; Atlas et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The VMPFC/OFC signal correlates negatively with the magnitude of aversive outcomes.
source: This is consistent with a large number of studies suggesting that the VMPFC/OFC represents a valenced outcome expectancy signal, which correlates positively with reward magnitude or the strength of appetitive outcomes (Montague and Berns, 2002; Rangel and Hare, 2010; Grabenhorst and Rolls, 2011; Clithero and Rangel, 2013), and correlates negatively with the magnitude of aversive outcomes (Schiller et al., 2008; Plassmann et al., 2010; Atlas et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The DLPFC has direct projections to the OFC.
source: The DLPFC has direct projections to the OFC (Yeterian et al., 2012) and rostral striatum (Haber, 2006), and is critical for rule maintenance, working memory, and cognitive control (Smith and Jonides, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yeterian et al., 2012.

claim: The DLPFC has direct projections to the rostral striatum.
source: The DLPFC has direct projections to the OFC (Yeterian et al., 2012) and rostral striatum (Haber, 2006), and is critical for rule maintenance, working memory, and cognitive control (Smith and Jonides, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Haber, 2006.

claim: The DLPFC is critical for rule maintenance, working memory, and cognitive control.
source: The DLPFC has direct projections to the OFC (Yeterian et al., 2012) and rostral striatum (Haber, 2006), and is critical for rule maintenance, working memory, and cognitive control (Smith and Jonides, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Smith and Jonides, 1999.

claim: One model of instructed reward learning posits that the DLPFC maintains instruction information and influences striatal processing through excitatory input.
source: One model of instructed reward learning posits that the DLPFC maintains instruction information and influences striatal processing through excitatory input (Doll et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Doll et al., 2009.

claim: The amygdala shows differential responses during aversive learning irrespective of contingency awareness.
source: Our findings are consistent with previous work indicating the amygdala shows differential responses during aversive learning irrespective of contingency awareness (Tabbert et al., 2011), and likewise that patients with unilateral temporal lobectomies exhibit differential SCRs during fear conditioning when they make expectancy ratings (Coppens et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Patients with unilateral temporal lobectomies exhibit differential SCRs during fear conditioning when they make expectancy ratings.
source: Our findings are consistent with previous work indicating the amygdala shows differential responses during aversive learning irrespective of contingency awareness (Tabbert et al., 2011), and likewise that patients with unilateral temporal lobectomies exhibit differential SCRs during fear conditioning when they make expectancy ratings (Coppens et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Coppens et al., 2009.

claim: When arousal is elicited by explicit information, differential SCRs seem to be mediated by pathways that bypass the amygdala.
source: Thus, when arousal is elicited by explicit information (e.g. through instruction or conscious expectancy), differential SCRs seem to be mediated by pathways that bypass the amygdala.
evidence: This is an inference from the findings of the study.

claim: The amygdala can be activated by instructed knowledge.
source: Studies of instructed fear and threat-related anxiety have examined the effects of instructions without reinforcement, and have shown that the amygdala can be activated by instructed knowledge (Phelps et al., 2001) and that left amygdala damage impairs the physiological expression of instructed fear (Funayama et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Phelps et al., 2001.

claim: Left amygdala damage impairs the physiological expression of instructed fear.
source: Studies of instructed fear and threat-related anxiety have examined the effects of instructions without reinforcement, and have shown that the amygdala can be activated by instructed knowledge (Phelps et al., 2001) and that left amygdala damage impairs the physiological expression of instructed fear (Funayama et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Funayama et al., 2001.

claim: The amygdala might be more attuned to instructed threat in the absence of aversive reinforcement.
source: Thus the amygdala might be more attuned to instructed threat in the absence of aversive reinforcement.
evidence: This is a speculation based on prior findings.

claim: Much of the activity in VMPFC/OFC reflects the computation of expected value.
source: In particular, previous work using fMRI, lesions, and electrophysiology indicates that much of the activity in VMPFC/OFC reflects the computation of expected value (Padoa-Schioppa and Assad, 2006; Clithero and Rangel, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Correlates of EV in amygdala and striatum may actually reflect associability and PE, respectively.
source: However, correlates of EV in amygdala and striatum may actually reflect two closely related quantities: associability (Pearce and Hall, 1980; Behrens et al., 2007; Li et al., 2011a; Zhang et al., 2016) and PE (Bayer and Glimcher, 2005; Li et al., 2011a; Zhang et al., 2016), respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies and theoretical work.

claim: The role of associability in models is to monitor the reliability of outcomes in the world so as to control the learning rate for separate experiential updating about predictions of those outcomes.
source: The role of associability in models is to monitor the reliability of outcomes in the world so as, in turn, to control the learning rate for separate experiential updating about predictions of those outcomes (Pearce and Hall, 1980; Behrens et al., 2007; Li et al., 2011a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: The vigilance of the amygdala-based signaling system may benefit survival, but might also run awry in conditions characterized by persistent fear, such as anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder.
source: The fact that amygdala-based signaling responds uniquely to threats, irrespective of instructions, might serve to prepare organisms to react to future threats in the environment. Though the vigilance of this system may benefit survival, it might also run awry in conditions characterized by persistent fear, such as anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder.
evidence: This is a speculation about clinical implications.

claim: The vigilance of the amygdala-based signaling system might underlie the critical role of experiential learning in successful therapy for anxiety and PTSD.
source: This might in turn underlie the critical role of experiential learning in successful therapy for these disorders.
evidence: This is a speculation about clinical implications.

claim: The neural computations that support feedback-driven learning are highly conserved across species, and rely heavily on the striatum, amygdala, and VMPFC/OFC.
source: It is clear that the neural computations that support feedback-driven learning are highly conserved across species, and rely heavily on the striatum, amygdala, and VMPFC/OFC.
evidence: This is a statement based on general knowledge of the literature.

claim: The strong influence of instructions on expected value coding in VMPFC/OFC may be consistent with the view that this region represents task state.
source: For example, the strong influence of instructions on expected value coding in VMPFC/OFC may be consistent with the view that this region represents task state (Wilson et al., 2013), which would update when individuals are told that contingencies change.
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citation to Wilson et al., 2013.

claim: The VMPFC/OFC has been shown to guide learning when value must be inferred.
